passages.title: Enamel, saliva and the daily balance of mineral
passages.text:
Enamel is the hardest tissue in the vertebrate body and, by weight, the least alive. A mature enamel cap is roughly ninety-six percent mineral, and the small remainder is divided between water and a sparse organic matrix. The cells that built it, the ameloblasts, finish their work before the tooth enters the mouth and are lost as the crown erupts. From that moment the tissue holds no resident cell, no blood supply and no nerve of its own. Whatever happens to enamel afterward happens by chemistry alone. That a structure with no capacity for cellular repair can survive fifty or sixty years of daily acid exposure is the puzzle this passage takes up.

The mineral itself belongs to the apatite family and is close in composition to hydroxyapatite, whose unit formula is written Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2. Millions of tiny crystallites are bundled into rods that run from the junction with the underlying dentin out to the surface. Chemically, the architecture matters less than a single fact: a crystal in contact with a watery fluid is never simply solid. Ions leave its surface and return to it continuously, and whether the crystal grows, holds steady or dissolves depends on how the concentrations of calcium, phosphate and hydroxide in the surrounding fluid compare with the concentrations the crystal would maintain at equilibrium. Enamel is best understood not as a wall but as a reservoir in exchange with the fluid that bathes it.

Acid tips that exchange. When hydrogen ions accumulate in the fluid at the enamel surface, they bind hydroxide and protonate phosphate, converting PO4 three-minus first to HPO4 two-minus and then to H2PO4 one-minus. Both reactions strip from solution the species the crystal needs to stay in balance. The fluid becomes undersaturated with respect to the mineral, and calcium and phosphate leave the crystal faster than they return. The pH at which the surrounding fluid crosses from supersaturated to undersaturated is called the critical pH. For hydroxyapatite bathed in ordinary plaque fluid it falls near 5.5, though that figure is not a constant of the mineral: it rises when the fluid is poor in calcium and phosphate and falls when the fluid is rich in them.

The acid does not arrive from outside. It is made on site, inside the soft bacterial film that colonises any tooth surface within hours of cleaning. Several species in that film ferment dietary sugars and release organic acids as waste, lactic acid chief among them. Because the film is a dense gel, the acid it produces is not immediately diluted by the far larger volume of saliva flowing past; instead it accumulates in the narrow space between the film and the enamel. Two teeth in one mouth, one recently cleaned and one covered by a mature film, therefore experience very different chemistry during the same meal.

The resulting pattern is a cycle rather than a steady state. Within two to five minutes of a sugar exposure the pH inside the film falls steeply. It reaches its minimum somewhere between five and twenty minutes after the exposure, then climbs back toward its resting value near neutrality over the following half hour to hour as acids diffuse away, are buffered, and are consumed. What decides the fate of the enamel underneath is not the depth of the trough alone but the total time the fluid spends below the critical pH. This is why the frequency of carbohydrate intake predicts mineral loss better than the quantity does: six small sweetened drinks spaced across a working day hold the surface below its critical pH far longer than one dessert containing the same total sugar.

Saliva is the counterweight. It is supersaturated with calcium and phosphate with respect to enamel mineral, so at rest it pushes ions toward the crystal rather than away from it. It clears sugars from the mouth mechanically, it dilutes and neutralises acid, and it buffers, chiefly through bicarbonate when flow is stimulated and through phosphate when flow is slow. Flow rate therefore governs how quickly the trough is climbed out of. Someone whose salivary output has been reduced, whether by a medication, by disease of the glands or by radiation delivered to the head and neck, spends far longer below the critical pH after each exposure than someone with normal flow, even on an identical diet.

Supersaturation raises an obvious difficulty: why does calcium phosphate not precipitate spontaneously throughout the mouth? The answer is a set of salivary proteins, among them statherin and the proline-rich proteins, that adsorb to mineral surfaces and inhibit uncontrolled crystal growth while leaving the ions themselves available. The same proteins deposit on a cleaned tooth within minutes as a thin film called the acquired pellicle, which slows the movement of acid toward the enamel and of dissolved mineral away from it. Saliva thus holds a mineral load in reserve rather than shedding it wherever the chemistry would otherwise allow.

Early attack does not look like erosion. Acid diffuses through the pores between crystallites and dissolves mineral in the body of the tissue, while the outermost layer, continually rebathed in supersaturated saliva, loses less and stays comparatively intact. The result is a subsurface lesion: a zone of mineral loss beneath a relatively sound surface. Clinically it appears as a chalky white patch, visible because the widened pores scatter light differently than sound enamel does. That surviving surface is what makes an early lesion interesting. It remains porous enough to admit ions from outside, so mineral can be driven back into the body of the lesion from the mouth.

Return, though, is not regeneration. Redeposited mineral grows on the surfaces of crystallites that survived the attack, using them as templates; nothing in the mouth can lay down new rods or restore the original architecture. So long as a scaffold of partly dissolved crystallites remains, repeated swings back toward supersaturation can rebuild a substantial fraction of the lost mineral, and the rebuilt tissue is often more resistant to the next episode than what it replaced. Once the crystallites in a region have dissolved completely and the surface collapses into a cavity, no chemistry can bridge the gap, and the defect has to be filled by a dentist.

Fluoride acts on both halves of the cycle. A fluoride ion is close in size to hydroxide and can substitute for it in the apatite lattice, producing fluorapatite, a mineral whose critical pH lies nearer 4.5 than 5.5 and which therefore tolerates acid episodes that would dissolve hydroxyapatite. Yet that lattice substitution is the smaller part of the benefit, because only a thin outer zone is ever converted. The larger effect is exerted from the fluid phase: fluoride present in saliva and plaque during an acid episode adsorbs to dissolving crystal surfaces, slows their dissolution, and speeds redeposition once the pH recovers. Frequent small exposures, such as a fluoride toothpaste used twice a day, therefore serve the tissue better than one large dose does, which is the reverse of the pattern that governs sugar.

The contrast with bone sharpens the point. Bone is a living composite that is continuously remodelled: cells resorb packets of mineralised matrix and other cells deposit new matrix in their place, so a fracture can be bridged and an unloaded region thinned and later rebuilt. Enamel has no such machinery. Its only repair is physicochemical, it can operate only where fluid reaches, and it depends entirely on the composition of that fluid rather than on any signal from the body. Enamel does not heal; the mouth around it either favours deposition or favours loss.

Seen this way, the familiar preventive measures are less a treatment than a way of tilting a balance. Spacing carbohydrate exposures shortens the total time spent below the critical pH; chewing after a meal, or sipping water, raises flow and speeds clearance; fluoride keeps a redepositing agent in place for the hour when the pH is recovering; removing the film removes the factory that makes the acid. None of this repairs a cavity, and none of it makes enamel alive. What it does is move a daily equilibrium in the direction of gain, and for a tissue that cannot repair itself, that modest shift, repeated three times a day for decades, is very nearly the whole of its defence.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a mature enamel cap is approximately what percentage mineral by weight?
options: About 60 percent
About 75 percent
About 85 percent
About 96 percent
About 99 percent
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph gives the figure directly: a mature cap is roughly ninety-six percent mineral, with the small remainder split between water and a sparse organic matrix. The tempting near-miss is ninety-nine percent, which leaves no room for the water and matrix the same sentence reserves.

distractors.why: Sixty percent is the kind of figure a cell-rich tissue would have; the first paragraph puts enamel far higher.
Seventy-five percent sounds right for a hard tissue in general, but it is not the number this paragraph states.
Eighty-five percent is close enough to feel safe if you remember only that enamel is "mostly mineral" and do not check the sentence.
Ninety-nine percent overshoots: the same sentence reserves a small remainder for water and an organic matrix.

questions.stem: The passage names which acid as the chief product of the bacterial film's fermentation of dietary sugars?
options: Lactic acid
Carbonic acid
Hydrochloric acid
Phosphoric acid
Sulfuric acid
questions.explanation: The paragraph on the film says the species in it ferment dietary sugars and release organic acids as waste, lactic acid chief among them. Phosphoric acid is the decoy, because phosphate appears all through the passage as a mineral ion rather than as a bacterial product.

distractors.why: Carbonic acid belongs to the bicarbonate buffering the passage credits to saliva, not to the bacteria in the film.
Hydrochloric acid is a stomach acid; the passage is explicit that the acid is made on site inside the film.
Phosphate is everywhere in this passage as a mineral ion, and it is easy to slide from phosphate to phosphoric acid, but a different acid is named as the chief waste product.
Sulfuric acid appears nowhere in the passage, and no sulfur chemistry is described anywhere in it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the critical pH for hydroxyapatite in ordinary plaque fluid falls near which value?
options: About 3.5
About 4.5
About 5.5
About 6.5
About 7.4
questions.explanation: The paragraph that defines the critical pH gives 5.5 for hydroxyapatite in ordinary plaque fluid. The value 4.5 is in the passage too, but it belongs to fluorapatite in the fluoride paragraph, which is what makes it the strongest decoy.

distractors.why: No figure this low appears anywhere in the passage.
This is the value the passage gives for fluorapatite, not for hydroxyapatite: a true number lifted from a different sentence.
A critical pH of 6.5 would put enamel on the edge of dissolving at rest, which contradicts the resting state the passage describes.
Near-neutral is where the passage says the cycle returns to, not the point at which the fluid turns undersaturated.

questions.stem: The passage mentions all of the following as ways saliva opposes mineral loss EXCEPT:
options: It clears sugars from the mouth mechanically and dilutes and neutralises acid.
It buffers acid through bicarbonate when flow is stimulated.
It buffers acid through phosphate when flow is slow.
It supplies calcium and phosphate in a supersaturated state.
It supplies antibodies that kill the bacteria that make the acid.
questions.explanation: The paragraph on saliva lists mechanical clearance, dilution and neutralisation, buffering by bicarbonate at stimulated flow and by phosphate at slow flow, and supersaturation with calcium and phosphate. An immune contribution is never mentioned, so that is the option the passage does not support.

distractors.why: Both halves sit in one sentence of the saliva paragraph, which says outright that saliva clears sugars mechanically and that it dilutes and neutralises acid, so this cannot be the exception.
Bicarbonate buffering at stimulated flow is named in the same sentence as phosphate buffering.
Phosphate buffering at slow flow is named explicitly; picking it usually means the two buffers were read as one.
Supersaturation with calcium and phosphate opens the saliva paragraph and is the reason saliva pushes ions toward the crystal.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what do statherin and the proline-rich proteins do?
options: Neutralise the acid in the film by buffering it
Inhibit uncontrolled crystal growth while leaving the ions available
Substitute for hydroxide ions inside the crystal lattice of the mineral
Raise the critical pH of the enamel mineral
Break down the bacterial film that produces the acid
questions.explanation: The paragraph answering why calcium phosphate does not precipitate everywhere says these proteins adsorb to mineral surfaces and inhibit uncontrolled crystal growth while leaving the ions themselves available. Buffering is credited to bicarbonate and phosphate a paragraph earlier, which is the decoy most readers take.

distractors.why: Buffering is real in this passage, but it is the work of bicarbonate and phosphate in the previous paragraph, not of these proteins.
Substituting for hydroxide in the lattice is what the passage says a fluoride ion does, three paragraphs later.
The passage does say the critical pH rises when the fluid is poor in calcium and phosphate, but it never credits that shift to these proteins.
Nothing in the passage gives these proteins any effect on the bacterial film.

questions.stem: Which sequence best describes what the passage says happens to the pH inside the film after a sugar exposure?
options: A gradual fall over about an hour, then a sudden return to neutrality once the sugar is cleared away.
A steep fall within two to five minutes, a minimum about an hour later, then a recovery over the following day.
A steep rise within two to five minutes, a maximum five to twenty minutes later, then a fall back toward neutrality over the next hour.
A steep fall within two to five minutes, a minimum five to twenty minutes later, then a climb back toward neutrality.
No change until the sugar has been cleared, then a fall that lasts until the next exposure begins.
questions.explanation: The cycle paragraph gives three landmarks in order: a steep fall within two to five minutes, a minimum five to twenty minutes after the exposure, then a climb back toward the resting value over the next half hour to hour. The reversal option keeps those timings but turns the fall into a rise.

distractors.why: The passage describes the fall as steep and quick, not gradual, and the recovery as slow rather than sudden.
The timings are stretched: the minimum comes five to twenty minutes after the exposure, and recovery takes under an hour.
This is the reversal trap: correct timings, wrong direction. Acid production lowers the pH inside the film rather than raising it.
The passage puts the steep fall within minutes of the exposure, long before the sugar has been cleared.

questions.stem: The passage attributes the chalky white appearance of an early lesion to which cause?
options: Bacterial pigment left on the surface of the enamel
Widened pores that scatter light differently than sound enamel
A collapsed surface that exposes the dentin underneath
A thickened layer of acquired pellicle over the area
Fluorapatite formed in the outer zone of the enamel
questions.explanation: The subsurface-lesion paragraph says the patch is visible because the widened pores scatter light differently than sound enamel does. A collapsed surface belongs to the cavitated lesion of the next paragraph, which is a different stage entirely.

distractors.why: No pigment of any kind is mentioned in the passage.
Collapse into a cavity is the later, irreversible stage described in the following paragraph, not the early white patch.
The pellicle is described as a thin film that slows diffusion; the passage never makes it visible.
Fluorapatite does form in a thin outer zone, but the passage offers it as acid resistance, not as the reason a lesion looks white.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which statement describes how bone differs from enamel?
options: Bone contains no organic matrix at all, whereas enamel retains a sparse one.
Bone begins to dissolve at a lower pH than enamel mineral does.
Bone depends on the composition of saliva for its supply of mineral.
Bone can be rebuilt only in the places an external fluid reaches.
Bone is remodelled by cells that resorb and deposit mineralised matrix.
questions.explanation: The comparison paragraph defines bone as a living composite that is continuously remodelled, with cells resorbing packets of mineralised matrix and other cells depositing new matrix. The option about rebuilding only where fluid reaches is a reversal: that limit is stated of enamel, not of bone.

distractors.why: Contradicted rather than unsupported: the comparison paragraph has cells resorbing packets of mineralised matrix and other cells depositing new matrix, so bone plainly has one. The trap is carrying enamel's sparse organic matrix across from the first paragraph and reading it as a contrast.
No critical pH is given for bone anywhere in the passage.
Dependence on the surrounding fluid is exactly what the passage says distinguishes enamel from bone.
This is the reversal: reaching only where fluid reaches is the limit the passage places on enamel repair.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: A tissue that cannot repair itself is maintained by a daily chemical balance of loss and return.
Fluoride is the single most important factor in preventing damage to the teeth.
Bacteria living in the film on the tooth are the cause of nearly all damage to enamel.
Enamel is built by specialised cells whose work before eruption decides how long a tooth will last.
Saliva performs a wider range of protective functions than most accounts of the mouth allow.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph poses the problem - a tissue with no cells that nevertheless lasts decades - and the last answers it by describing preventive measures as a way of tilting a daily balance. Every other option names a real element of the passage and promotes it to the whole.

distractors.why: Fluoride gets one paragraph, and the passage is careful to call the lattice substitution the smaller part of its benefit.
The film supplies the acid, but the passage devotes as much space to the saliva and mineral chemistry that oppose it.
The ameloblasts appear once, and only to establish that they are gone before the story of the passage begins.
Saliva is one half of the balance the passage describes, which makes this a true statement about a part rather than the whole.

questions.stem: Paragraph 4 opens by saying that the acid does not arrive from outside. That sentence serves mainly to:
options: concede that what a person eats matters less to mineral loss than the passage has claimed
explain why the critical pH is not a fixed constant of the enamel mineral itself
give the acid of the previous paragraph a source: a film that makes it on the tooth
argue that a tooth cleaned this morning and one left uncleaned meet the same chemistry
announce saliva as the counterweight that the paragraph immediately after will describe
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 describes what acid does to the crystal but never says where the acid comes from. The opening sentence of paragraph 4 is the hinge that supplies it, and the rest of the paragraph delivers the answer: a bacterial film on the tooth that ferments dietary sugars and traps its own waste acid against the enamel. The strongest decoy reverses the paragraph's closing sentence.

distractors.why: Nothing is conceded about diet; the paragraph after this one makes the frequency of carbohydrate intake the best predictor of mineral loss the passage offers.
That explanation is already finished in paragraph 3, which says the critical pH rises in a fluid poor in calcium and phosphate and falls in one rich in them.
The reversal trap: the paragraph closes on two teeth in one mouth, one recently cleaned and one covered by a mature film, experiencing very different chemistry.
Saliva is two paragraphs away, and the paragraph immediately after this one is the pH cycle rather than the counterweight.

questions.stem: What purpose does the question that opens paragraph 7 serve?
options: It casts doubt on the claim that saliva is supersaturated at rest.
It signals that the author is leaving the chemistry of enamel behind.
It restates the main idea of the passage in the form of a question.
It raises the objection that fluoride would be unnecessary in a mouth with healthy saliva.
It sets up the salivary proteins that hold mineral in solution until it is needed.
questions.explanation: The question asks why supersaturated saliva does not precipitate everywhere, and the sentence immediately after it answers with statherin and the proline-rich proteins. It is a setup for the paragraph's own content, not a challenge to what came before.

distractors.why: Supersaturation is not doubted: the paragraph takes it as given and explains how it is kept under control.
The paragraph stays inside the same chemistry, explaining how the mineral load is held in reserve.
The main idea is the balance between loss and return; this question is narrower than that.
Fluoride is not mentioned until several paragraphs later and is never called unnecessary.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be the most appropriate title for the passage?
options: The Bacteria Behind Tooth Decay
Enamel Under Acid: A Balance of Loss and Return
How Fluoride Reshaped Preventive Dentistry
Building the Crown: What the Ameloblasts Leave Behind
Saliva: The Body's Most Underrated Fluid
questions.explanation: A title has to cover the whole passage, and the whole passage is about mineral leaving and returning to a tissue that cannot repair itself. The other titles each name a supporting player - the film, fluoride, the ameloblasts, saliva - and would leave most of the text unaccounted for.

distractors.why: The film is the source of the acid, but it occupies one paragraph of twelve.
Fluoride is treated as one contributor to the balance, and no history of dentistry is offered.
The ameloblasts are mentioned only to say they are gone before the tooth erupts.
Saliva is half the story at most, and the passage never compares it with other fluids of the body.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the preventive measures described in the final paragraph is best described as:
options: Enthusiastic and promotional
Openly alarmed by the risk
Dismissive of their value
Measured, with qualified optimism
Resigned and pessimistic about prevention
questions.explanation: The last paragraph endorses the measures and in the same breath limits them: none repairs a cavity, none makes enamel alive, and what they achieve is a modest shift in a daily equilibrium. Endorsement plus stated limits is measured optimism rather than enthusiasm.

distractors.why: An enthusiast would not spend the closing sentences on what the measures cannot do.
The tone stays analytic throughout; no language of alarm appears.
Dismissal is ruled out by the claim that this modest shift is very nearly the whole of the defence.
Pessimism is ruled out by the same claim, and by the earlier statement that rebuilt tissue is often more resistant.

questions.stem: Which of the following must be true according to the passage?
options: Splitting the same quantity of sugar into more exposures can increase mineral loss.
Any exposure to sugar will eventually produce a cavity somewhere in the enamel.
Enamel that has lost mineral can never regain any part of it.
Saliva by itself is enough to prevent all loss of mineral in a mouth that is healthy.
A person who avoids sugar entirely has no need of fluoride.
questions.explanation: The cycle paragraph says outright that what matters is the total time below the critical pH, and that six spaced drinks keep the surface below it longer than one dessert of the same total sugar. That makes the effect of splitting a fixed quantity something the passage forces, not merely permits.

distractors.why: The passage never says every exposure ends in a cavity; it describes a balance that usually recovers.
Flatly contradicted: mineral can be driven back into a lesion while crystallite templates survive.
Too strong. Saliva opposes loss, but the passage gives a whole cycle in which loss still happens.
The passage gives fluoride a role in redeposition that does not depend on the diet being sugary.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which conclusion about a lesion that has collapsed into a cavity?
options: It will go on losing mineral faster than an intact enamel surface does.
It can still be reversed if fluoride is supplied often enough.
It cannot be rebuilt, because the crystallite templates are gone.
It shows that the patient's saliva was never supersaturated with mineral.
It scatters light in the way an early white patch on enamel does.
questions.explanation: Redeposition is described as growth on surviving crystallites used as templates, and the passage states that once the crystallites of a region have dissolved completely no chemistry can bridge the gap. The fluoride option is the trap for a reader who remembers that fluoride speeds redeposition but not what redeposition requires.

distractors.why: The passage stops at the defect having to be filled by a dentist and never compares rates of loss between a cavity and an intact surface; the pull is the intuition that a cavity is a wound that keeps getting worse, which the passage neither states nor needs.
Fluoride speeds redeposition onto surviving crystallites; where none survive, the passage says the defect must be filled.
Supersaturation is described as the normal resting state of saliva, and no link is drawn to an individual failing.
Light scattering is offered for the early white patch, which the passage distinguishes from a collapsed surface.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, which person is at greatest risk of losing enamel mineral?
options: A patient on a medication that reduces salivary flow who sips a sweetened drink all afternoon
A patient with normal salivary flow who eats one large dessert after dinner each evening
A patient with normal salivary flow who drinks water between meals and brushes twice a day
A patient with unusually high salivary flow who eats one sweetened snack at breakfast
A patient whose teeth were cleaned this morning and who eats no carbohydrate all day
questions.explanation: Two factors in the passage both point the same way: many spaced exposures keep the surface below the critical pH longer than one large one, and reduced salivary flow lengthens every recovery. The patient who combines them spends the most time on the losing side of the balance.

distractors.why: One large exposure with normal flow is the passage's own example of the lower-risk pattern.
Water between meals aids clearance, and nothing here prolongs the time below the critical pH.
High flow shortens each recovery, and a single snack gives only one trough to climb out of.
With no carbohydrate there is nothing for the film to ferment, so no acid episode begins.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the passage's claim that the frequency of carbohydrate intake matters more than the quantity?
options: Plaque films differ in thickness from one tooth to the next within a single mouth.
Six small sugar portions and one large portion produced equal time below the critical pH.
People who took sugar six times a day lost more mineral than people who took it once.
Sweetened drinks lower the pH in the film faster than solid sweets of the same sugar content.
Salivary flow rate varies more between individuals than plaque acid production does.
questions.explanation: The claim rests on a mechanism: splitting the same sugar into more exposures lengthens the total time below the critical pH. A result in which spacing leaves that total unchanged removes the mechanism and with it the claim.

distractors.why: Variation between teeth says nothing about how spacing a fixed quantity of sugar changes the time below the critical pH.
This is the reversal trap: it is the result the claim predicts, so it strengthens the claim rather than weakening it.
A difference in how fast the pH falls compares forms of sugar, not the frequency of exposure against the quantity.
How flow rate varies between people leaves the frequency-versus-quantity comparison untouched.

passages.title: Why brittle solids break far below their bonds
passages.text:
A chemist who knows the strength of a silicon-oxygen bond can estimate how strong a pane of glass ought to be. Stretch a flawless solid until its planes of atoms separate, and the stress required comes out at roughly one tenth of the material's Young's modulus, the constant relating stress to elastic stretch. For ordinary window glass the modulus is about seventy gigapascals, so the bonds predict a breaking stress near seven gigapascals. A sheet of window glass, pulled apart in a laboratory, breaks closer to fifty megapascals. The prediction misses by more than a factor of a hundred. A discrepancy that large and that consistent is not an arithmetic error; the bond calculation is answering a different question than the engineer's.

The resolution begins with a geometric observation about loaded bodies that contain holes. For an elliptical hole in a large plate, with the long axis of the ellipse lying across the direction of pull, the stress at the sharp end exceeds the average stress in the plate by a factor of one plus twice the ratio of the two semi-axes. A round hole, whose axes are equal, therefore triples the local stress. A narrow slit whose length is a hundred times its width multiplies it by two hundred and one. A scratch a tenth of a millimetre long and a micrometre wide is, arithmetically, exactly such a slit.

Stress concentration explains why flaws are dangerous, but taken alone it explains too much. Push the ratio of the axes toward a perfectly sharp crack and the predicted local stress grows without limit, which would mean that no cracked body could carry any load whatever. The stress at a crack tip therefore cannot by itself be the criterion for failure. Something else must decide whether a crack already present will begin to run.

The criterion that works is an energy balance rather than a stress comparison. A loaded plate stores elastic energy; when a crack extends, the material just above and below the new crack faces unloads and gives that energy back, while the extension creates fresh surface, and surface costs energy to make. The crack grows if, and only if, the energy released by unloading exceeds the energy the new surface demands. The two terms scale differently: the energy released per unit of crack extension rises with the square of the applied stress and in proportion to the length the crack has already reached, while the surface cost per unit of extension is a constant of the material.

Working that balance through yields the relation that governs brittle solids. The stress at which an existing crack begins to run is proportional to the square root of the material's modulus multiplied by its surface energy, and inversely proportional to the square root of the crack's length. Strength therefore falls off as the square root of flaw size, so a flaw four times longer halves the stress a part can carry. The relation is unforgiving in one direction and generous in the other: shrinking the worst flaw by a factor of a hundred multiplies the strength by ten. It also accounts for the missing factor of a hundred in the first paragraph.

Three consequences follow. The first is that the strength of a brittle part is a property of its worst flaw rather than of its average condition. Two panes off the same line can differ in strength by a factor of several if one carries a deeper scratch. A glass fibre drawn fresh from a melt and never touched can reach several gigapascals, close to what the bond calculation predicts, because it has no surface damage at all. Draw that same fibre once across a wooden bench and its strength falls by an order of magnitude. Nothing about the glass changed; its worst flaw did.

The second consequence is statistical. Flaws are scattered over a surface with some distribution of sizes, and a larger specimen samples that distribution more times, so the expected size of its worst flaw is larger. Brittle materials therefore appear to grow weaker as the piece grows bigger. A long glass rod breaks at a lower stress than a short one cut from the same stock, an effect owing nothing to the material and everything to sampling. Engineers accordingly describe a brittle material with a distribution of strengths rather than a single number, designing against the stress at which perhaps one part in ten thousand fails.

The third consequence is that strength is the wrong constant to tabulate. Rearranged, the relation says that failure occurs when the applied stress multiplied by the square root of the crack length reaches a value fixed by the material. That product is the fracture toughness, and unlike strength it belongs to the material rather than to the specimen. Quoted in megapascals times the square root of a metre, it ranges widely: about 0.7 for soda-lime glass, about 3.5 for alumina, near 30 for a common aluminium alloy, near 50 for structural steel.

Toughness matters in design because it fixes the crack size a part can tolerate. Invert the relation and the critical crack length at a given service stress comes out proportional to the square of the toughness. Two parts carrying the same stress, one steel and one glass, therefore tolerate crack lengths in the ratio of the squares of their toughness values, roughly five thousand to one. The steel part can be scratched, dented and left with a flaw a millimetre long and still carry its load; the glass part is endangered by a flaw too small to see. That ratio, not any difference in bond strength, is what an engineer means by calling steel tough and glass brittle.

The mechanism behind the gap is plastic flow at the crack tip. In a metal, the concentrated stress ahead of a crack exceeds the yield stress, so a small zone of material deforms permanently instead of separating. The deformation blunts the tip, which lowers the concentration, and it dissipates energy: the work absorbed per unit of new crack area runs to hundreds or thousands of times the energy of the two fresh surfaces alone. A brittle ceramic at room temperature has no comparable outlet. Its crack tip stays sharp and its energy budget stays close to the bare surface term.

Three engineering responses follow, each attacking a different term. The first is to control the flaws: polish, etch, coat, inspect and handle carefully; the strength recovered goes only as the square root of the reduction achieved, so halving the worst flaw buys about forty per cent more strength, not double. The second is to change the stress the flaw actually feels. Tempered glass is cooled so that its surfaces end in compression, typically around a hundred megapascals; an applied tension must cancel that compression before any surface flaw sees a positive stress at all. Chemically strengthened glass reaches the same end by exchanging small ions in the surface layer for larger ones. The third is to test before service: a proof test loads every part above its working stress, and a part that survives cannot contain a crack longer than the critical size for that stress.

None of this makes a brittle part safe in the way a ductile one is. A steel beam loaded past its limit sags and gives warning; a glass panel gives none, because the same balance that sets its strength also guarantees that once a crack passes the critical length the released energy exceeds the surface cost by a widening margin, and the crack accelerates to a large fraction of the speed of sound. The design philosophy that follows is procedural rather than heroic. Choose for toughness rather than for headline strength, keep the service stress low enough that the critical crack is long enough to find by inspection, and set the inspection interval by how fast a crack is expected to grow. An engineer who answers a fracture by specifying a stronger grade of steel, without asking what flaw the failure started from, is answering the bond chemist's question instead of the engineering one.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the breaking stress that a bond-based calculation predicts for ordinary window glass is about
options: 50 megapascals
70 megapascals
7 gigapascals
70 gigapascals
100 megapascals
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 puts the modulus of window glass near seventy gigapascals and the bond-based strength at roughly one tenth of it, which is seven gigapascals. The fifty megapascals in the same paragraph is the trap: it is what a real sheet does, not what the bonds predict.

distractors.why: Decoy: fifty megapascals is in the paragraph, but it is the measured breaking stress, which is the other half of the comparison.
Half-right: it borrows the number seventy from the modulus and the unit from the measured strength, so neither half belongs to the prediction.
Decoy: seventy gigapascals is the modulus itself; the predicted strength is one tenth of that value.
Decoy: a hundred megapascals appears later as the surface compression in tempered glass, which answers a different question.

questions.stem: The passage states that a round hole in a large loaded plate raises the stress at the edge of the hole to
options: Three times the average stress in the plate
Twice the average stress in the plate
The same value as the average stress in the plate
Two hundred and one times the average stress in the plate
Ten times the average stress in the plate
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 gives the factor as one plus twice the ratio of the semi-axes. A round hole has equal axes, so the ratio is one and the factor is three. The usual trap is to keep the doubling and forget the added one.

distractors.why: Half-right: it uses the 'twice the ratio' half of the rule and drops the 'one plus' that the same sentence supplies.
Reversal: the paragraph exists to say that stress crowds at a hole rather than staying at its average value.
Decoy: two hundred and one is the factor the same paragraph gives for a slit a hundred times longer than it is wide.
This figure appears nowhere in the passage; it is a guess at a round number rather than a reading of the rule.

questions.stem: The fracture toughness the passage reports for soda-lime glass, in megapascals times the square root of a metre, is about
questions.explanation: Paragraph 8 lists four toughness values and puts soda-lime glass at about 0.7. The other three values in the list belong to alumina, an aluminium alloy and structural steel.

distractors.why: This number is not in the list; it is half the glass value, and nothing in the paragraph asks for a halving.
Decoy: 3.5 is the value the same sentence gives for alumina, which is a ceramic but not the one asked about.
Decoy: 30 is the value given for a common aluminium alloy.
Decoy: 50 is the value given for structural steel, the material the later paragraphs contrast with glass.

questions.stem: According to the passage, chemically strengthened glass puts its surface into compression by
options: Cooling the surfaces so that they end in compression
Coating the surface with a thin polymer film
Etching the surface to remove the deepest flaws
Exchanging small ions in the surface layer for larger ones
Loading every part above its working stress before service
questions.explanation: Paragraph 11 distinguishes two ways of putting a surface into compression: thermal tempering, which cools the surfaces, and chemical strengthening, which swaps small surface ions for larger ones. The cooling option is the trap because it is the neighbouring sentence.

distractors.why: Decoy: cooling is true of the passage, but it is how tempered glass is made, not how chemically strengthened glass is made.
A polymer coating appears nowhere in the passage; coating is mentioned only in the list of ways to limit flaw size.
Decoy: etching is in the same paragraph, but under controlling flaws rather than under putting the surface in compression.
Decoy: loading above the working stress is the proof test, the third response in the same paragraph.

questions.stem: The passage puts the ratio of the crack lengths that steel and glass can tolerate at the same service stress at roughly
options: Seventy to one
Seven hundred to one
Five thousand to one
One hundred to one
Fifty to one
questions.explanation: Paragraph 9 says the tolerable crack length goes as the square of the toughness, and gives the steel-to-glass ratio as roughly five thousand to one. Dividing the two toughness values without squaring them is what produces the near-seventy figure.

distractors.why: Half-right: seventy is the ratio of the two toughness values, but the paragraph says the crack length follows the square of the toughness.
This is neither the ratio of the toughness values nor its square; it sits between the two and matches nothing in the paragraph.
Decoy: a factor of a hundred is the gap between the predicted and measured strength of glass in the opening paragraphs.
Decoy: fifty is the toughness quoted for structural steel, not a ratio of crack lengths.

questions.stem: The passage names all of the following as ways engineers respond to the risk of brittle fracture EXCEPT
options: Polishing and inspecting surfaces to limit flaw size
Cooling a glass surface so that it ends in compression
Loading every part above its working stress before service
Alloying a material to raise its Young's modulus
Keeping the service stress low enough that a critical crack can be found
questions.explanation: Paragraph 11 lists flaw control, surface compression and proof testing, and paragraph 12 adds keeping the service stress low enough for inspection to work. Raising the modulus by alloying is never proposed; the modulus enters the relation, but the passage treats flaw size and toughness as the levers.

distractors.why: Decoy: polishing and inspecting open the list of flaw-control measures, so this is verifiable and therefore not the answer.
Decoy: this is thermal tempering, stated in the same paragraph as a way to change the stress a flaw feels.
Decoy: this is the proof test, the third response named in that paragraph.
Decoy: the closing paragraph recommends exactly this, so it is in the passage and cannot be the exception.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which sequence describes what happens in a brittle panel once a crack passes the critical length?
options: The tip blunts, a plastic zone forms, and the crack stops
The energy released outruns the surface cost, and the crack accelerates
The surface cost outruns the energy released, and the crack arrests
The applied stress falls to the bond-based strength, and the crack stops
Surface compression cancels the applied tension, and the crack closes
questions.explanation: The closing paragraph says that past the critical length the released energy exceeds the surface cost by a widening margin and the crack accelerates to a large fraction of the speed of sound, which is the order the energy balance of paragraph 4 predicts.

distractors.why: Decoy: blunting by a plastic zone is described, but for metals, and it is what keeps a crack from reaching this stage.
Reversal: the two terms are swapped, which describes a crack below the critical length rather than past it.
The applied stress does not fall as the crack runs, and the bond-based strength plays no part after the opening paragraph.
Decoy: surface compression belongs to tempered glass in the engineering-responses paragraph, not to a crack already running.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Brittle solids fail far below their bond-based strength because the largest flaw present, not the bonding, fixes when a crack runs
Glass is weaker than steel because silicon-oxygen bonds are weaker than the bonds in metals
The stress concentrated at a sharp hole is the criterion that decides whether a loaded part fails
Because the strength of a brittle part cannot be predicted at all, engineers have no choice but to test every single part that they intend to put into service
Thermal tempering and ion exchange are the most effective ways of making glass usable in engineering structures
questions.explanation: The passage opens with the gap between predicted and measured strength, resolves it with an energy balance in which strength falls as the square root of flaw size, and then draws the design consequences. Flaw size, not bond strength, is the thread.

distractors.why: Reversal of the passage's own conclusion: it states explicitly that the steel-glass contrast is not a difference in bond strength.
Half-right: stress concentration is introduced as the explanation, then rejected because it would predict that no cracked body carries any load.
Too strong: proof testing is one of three responses, and the passage predicts strength well enough to design against a one-in-ten-thousand failure stress.
Decoy: surface compression is a true detail of one paragraph, not the claim the whole passage builds.

questions.stem: The last five paragraphs of the passage are chiefly concerned with
options: Explaining why the bonds in glass are weaker than the bonds in steel
Describing the apparatus used in a laboratory to measure fracture toughness
Arguing that brittle materials ought to be withdrawn from every load-bearing application in engineering
Comparing the surface energies measured for various ceramics and metals
Turning the flaw-size relation into rules for choosing, treating and inspecting parts
questions.explanation: Paragraphs 8 to 12 move from the toughness constant to tolerable crack size, then to why metals are tough, then to the three engineering responses and the design philosophy. That is the relation being converted into practice.

distractors.why: Reversal: the passage denies that bond strength explains the contrast, so this cannot be what those paragraphs argue.
No apparatus is described anywhere; toughness is given as a tabulated constant, not as a measurement procedure.
Too strong: the closing paragraph gives rules for using brittle parts safely rather than for abandoning them.
Half-right: surface energy appears in the relation and in the discussion of plastic flow, but no comparison of measured surface energies is offered.

questions.stem: The description of the elliptical hole in the second paragraph functions mainly to
options: Supply a formula readers can use to calculate the strength of a cracked part
Recommend that holes in engineering parts be made round wherever possible
Establish that a small flaw can multiply the local stress enormously
Show that the bond calculation of the first paragraph was arithmetically wrong
Introduce the fracture toughness that later paragraphs tabulate for four different materials
questions.explanation: The elliptical-hole factor is what makes a scratch dangerous, and the paragraph ends by pointing out that an ordinary scratch is arithmetically such a slit. The next paragraph then withdraws it as a failure criterion, so it is a step in the argument rather than the answer.

distractors.why: Half-right: a formula is given, but the following paragraph says it cannot fix a failure stress, since a sharp crack would make the predicted stress unbounded.
No such recommendation appears; the round hole is an illustration of the factor, not advice about design.
Reversal: the first paragraph says the discrepancy is not an arithmetic error but a sign that the calculation answers another question.
Decoy: fracture toughness is real and tabulated, but it arrives six paragraphs later and by way of the energy balance.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best title for the passage?
options: The Worst Flaw: Why Brittle Solids Break Far Below Their Bonds
Young's Modulus and the Elastic Behaviour of Ceramic Materials
Tempered Glass: Surface Compression and Its Uses
Plastic Flow and the Toughness of Structural Metals
Why Engineers Should Never Specify a Brittle Material for a Load-Bearing Part
questions.explanation: A title has to cover the opening puzzle, the flaw-size relation and the design consequences. Only the worst-flaw title does; the rest name a single paragraph or overstate the conclusion.

distractors.why: The modulus is one term in one relation and elastic behaviour is never the subject; this titles a different article.
Decoy: tempering is one sentence of the engineering-responses paragraph, not the passage's subject.
Decoy: plastic flow occupies one paragraph and is there to explain why metals differ from ceramics.
Too strong: the passage sets out how to use brittle materials safely rather than telling engineers to avoid them.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward an engineer who answers a fracture failure by specifying a stronger grade of steel is best described as
options: Openly enthusiastic
Pointedly critical
Carefully neutral
Alarmed and urgent
Mildly approving
questions.explanation: The final sentence says such an engineer is answering the bond chemist's question instead of the engineering one, which is a pointed criticism made in the passage's otherwise measured voice.

distractors.why: The closing sentence is a rebuke; nothing in it endorses the practice, let alone with enthusiasm.
Half-right: the passage is measured throughout, but this last sentence takes a clear position rather than withholding one.
Overstated: the paragraph recommends inspection intervals and low service stresses in a calm procedural voice, not an alarm.
Reversal: approval is the opposite of what the sentence expresses.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly implies that a glass fibre dragged once across a wooden bench loses strength because
options: Friction heats the fibre and weakens its bonds
Abrasion reduces the fibre's cross-section and so raises the stress it carries
Contact with any solid surface always lowers a material's Young's modulus
Every flaw in a brittle solid grows steadily once the material has been handled at all, whatever stress it is under
The handling leaves surface flaws larger than any it previously contained
questions.explanation: The paragraph says the fresh fibre is strong because it has no surface damage, and that after the drag nothing about the glass changed except its worst flaw. Combined with the square-root relation, a larger worst flaw is the only account the passage supports.

distractors.why: Heating and bond weakening are nowhere in the passage, which says explicitly that nothing about the glass itself changed.
Half-right: abrasion is real, but a cross-section small enough to matter is never claimed, and the passage attributes the loss to the worst flaw.
Too strong and unsupported: the modulus is treated as a fixed property of the material throughout.
Too strong: an absolute claim about steady growth under any stress, where the passage says a crack runs only once the energy balance turns.

questions.stem: Two plates of the same glass are alike except that the worst flaw in the second is nine times as long as the worst flaw in the first. The passage implies that the second plate will fail at about
options: One ninth the stress of the first
One half the stress of the first
One third the stress of the first
Three times the stress of the first
The same stress as the first, since the material is unchanged
questions.explanation: Strength falls as the square root of flaw size, so nine times the flaw length divides the strength by the square root of nine, which is three. The passage's own example, a fourfold flaw halving the strength, is the same rule at a different number.

distractors.why: It treats strength as inversely proportional to flaw length; the relation given is inverse to the square root of that length.
Decoy: halving is what the passage's worked example gives for a flaw four times longer, not nine times longer.
Reversal: a longer flaw makes a part weaker, so the ratio runs the other way.
Contradicted: the whole point of the paragraph is that two plates of one material differ in strength when their worst flaws differ.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the passage's explanation of why larger brittle specimens are weaker?
options: Freshly drawn glass fibres are found to be stronger than any pane of the same glass
Larger panes are found, on inspection, to carry more and deeper surface scratches than smaller panes of the same glass
Fracture toughness is found to be the same whatever the size of the specimen tested
Specimens of very different size, each carrying one identical artificial flaw and no others, still fail at very different stresses
Tempered panes are found to be stronger than untempered panes of the same size
questions.explanation: The passage explains the size effect purely by sampling: a bigger specimen is likelier to contain a bigger worst flaw. Holding the flaw population identical and still seeing a size effect leaves that explanation with nothing to do.

distractors.why: Consistent with the passage rather than against it, since the fibre's strength is credited to its undamaged surface.
Reversal of the task: more and deeper scratches in larger panes is exactly the sampling account, so this supports the explanation.
The passage already treats toughness as a property of the material rather than of the specimen, so this changes nothing.
Decoy: a true-sounding result about surface compression that says nothing about specimen size.

questions.stem: A designer must choose between two materials for a panel that will be handled in service and must carry a fixed stress. Based on the passage, which question should weigh most heavily?
options: Which material has the higher Young's modulus
Which material has the higher bond-based theoretical strength
Which material has the lower surface energy
Which material can be produced in a larger single piece
Which material tolerates the longer crack at that stress
questions.explanation: Handling puts flaws in, and the passage's rule for that case is to choose for toughness rather than headline strength, because toughness fixes the crack length a part can carry at a given stress.

distractors.why: Half-right: the modulus is one term in the relation, but the rule the passage gives for a part that will be handled is toughness, which is what fixes the tolerable crack length at a given stress.
Contradicted: the opening and closing paragraphs both treat the bond-based figure as the wrong question for a real part.
Reversal: a lower surface energy means the crack costs less to extend, which lowers the stress the part can carry.
Reversal: the passage says larger pieces of a brittle material are weaker, so this points the wrong way.

passages.contentNote: Original expository passage written for this track from established materials-science results; no published passage, item or figure is reproduced, and the science is presented so that every question is answerable from the text alone.
