passages.title: How chemists settled on a reference for atomic weights
passages.text:
A unit of measurement is a promise. It promises that a quantity reported in one laboratory means the same thing in another, and that a number written down this year will mean the same a century from now. Keeping that promise is hard, because a unit must be anchored to something, and everything in nature turns out to be more complicated than it looks. The history of the atomic weight scale, the ladder of relative masses on which chemistry's bookkeeping rests, is worth following for that reason. It shows a scientific community arguing itself, slowly and with some embarrassment, toward a standard nobody would have chosen for its elegance and everybody could live with.

An atomic weight is not a mass in grams. It is a ratio: a statement that an atom of one element is so many times heavier than an atom of some other element chosen as the reference. Early chemists could not weigh a single atom, but they could weigh the quantities of two elements that combined, and from those combining weights they could work out relative masses. Ratios, however, need a denominator. Before anyone could say that carbon is twelve times something, the community had to agree on what the something was. That agreement was a convention rather than a discovery, and a century of use did not make it less of one.

The first convention was the obvious one. Hydrogen is the lightest element, and the earliest table of relative weights, drawn up in the opening years of the nineteenth century, gave it the value one so that every other element would come out greater than one. Elegance and practice parted company almost at once. Hydrogen combines with only a modest range of elements, and the compounds it does form are often gases that were awkward to trap and weigh with the equipment of the period. A chemist fixing the relative weight of a metal through hydrogen usually had to work through two or three intermediate compounds, and every extra step added error.

Oxygen was the practical alternative. It combines with nearly every element, often in compounds that are stable solids, easily purified and easily weighed, so most relative weights could be fixed against oxygen in a single step. A Swedish chemist of the same period built his tables on oxygen at one hundred. That figure did not survive. By the end of the century the community had settled on sixteen instead, for the unsentimental reason that sixteen left hydrogen at very nearly one and so preserved the familiar look of the tables already in print. The reference had changed; the numbers chemists had memorized had not. A standard succeeds partly by not disturbing the work already done.

For some thirty years the arrangement gave no trouble, and it is worth being precise about why. Oxygen at sixteen worked because everyone tacitly assumed that a chemical element is a single kind of atom, so that every oxygen atom weighs what every other oxygen atom weighs and a sample from one source is interchangeable with any other. The assumption was never stated as a premise, because nobody saw that it was one. Standards tend to hide their assumptions in this way. An assumption stays invisible for as long as it happens to be true, and becomes visible only when an instrument arrives sensitive enough to violate it.

The instrument arrived as precise spectroscopic analysis of ordinary air, and in 1929 the assumption failed. Oxygen, it emerged, is not one kind of atom but three. Atoms of the same element always carry the same number of protons, which is what makes them that element and fixes their chemistry, but they may carry different numbers of neutrons, which changes their mass. Variants of this sort are called isotopes. Ordinary oxygen is overwhelmingly the lightest of its three isotopes, but a small and, crucially, not perfectly constant fraction of any sample consists of the two heavier ones. The reference substance of chemistry was a mixture whose recipe depended on where it had been collected.

The response split the sciences. Physicists, who could by then separate the isotopes, did the clean thing and redefined the scale on a single isotope: the lightest oxygen atom, taken as exactly sixteen. Chemists, whose analyses deal with bulk samples in which the isotopes are never separated, kept the older reference, the natural mixture, also taken as exactly sixteen. Two scales now existed under one name. They were not far apart, the physical values running higher than the chemical ones by roughly two hundred and seventy-five parts per million, a discrepancy of about three hundredths of a percent, but they were not the same, and a value copied from one literature into the other was quietly wrong.

It is tempting to wave away a disagreement of that size, and for most bench work it did not matter; a chemist weighing out reagents would never have noticed. The serious objection was of another kind. Because the isotopic composition of natural oxygen varies slightly with its source, oxygen from the atmosphere being not quite oxygen from seawater and neither quite oxygen from a mineral, the chemists' reference was not a fixed quantity at all. Its value drifted according to which bottle you happened to open. A standard that cannot be reproduced exactly is not a standard; it is a habit. That, and not the size of the gap, is what forced a decision.

Two remedies were tried first, and both were evasions. The simpler was to publish conversion factors, so that a physicist's value could be turned into a chemist's. This works, in the sense that arithmetic always works, but a conversion factor between two versions of the same quantity is a confession rather than a solution, and it guarantees that somebody will eventually forget to apply it. The second remedy was for each discipline to argue that the other should give way. The physicists pointed out, correctly, that only a single isotope can serve as an exact reference. The chemists pointed out, also correctly, that a scale nobody will use is worth nothing.

The proposal that broke the deadlock, made in the late nineteen-fifties, satisfied both objections by abandoning oxygen altogether. Let the reference be carbon, and specifically the common carbon isotope with twelve particles in its nucleus, assigned the value twelve exactly. It is a single isotope, so it is exactly reproducible and the physicists' principle is honoured. It was already the working reference inside mass spectrometry, where carbon-bearing fragments make convenient markers. And, decisive for the chemists, the shift it demanded was tiny: moving from the old chemical scale to the carbon scale altered published atomic weights by about forty parts per million, far below the precision of most tabulated values, so the tables could stand.

The international union of physicists adopted the carbon standard in 1960 and the union of chemists in 1961, and the two scales became one. What deserves attention is the shape of the winning argument. It was not the most principled proposal, nor the one urged by the more powerful discipline. It was the proposal that asked each side for a small and bearable loss. The physicists gave up oxygen, on which their exact scale had been built; the chemists accepted a revision of every atomic weight in print, which they could afford only because the revision was too small to matter. A proposal that makes one community bear the whole cost of agreement does not get adopted, however sound it is.

The direction of travel since then has been consistent. Where an early standard was a substance, a bottle of gas or a bar of metal in a vault, a modern one is increasingly a number fixed by agreement, rebuilt by anyone with adequate apparatus. The unit chemists use to count particles followed in 2019, when it stopped being defined by a stated mass of carbon and was defined instead by fixing the number of entities it contains. Carbon at twelve remains the anchor of the atomic weight scale, but counting no longer depends on possessing any carbon. The purpose of a standard, the oxygen episode taught, is not to be natural or beautiful but to be rebuildable, by strangers, from written instructions alone.

questions.stem: According to the passage, chemists eventually replaced oxygen's assigned value of one hundred with sixteen because sixteen:
options: matched the value that physicists later gave to the lightest oxygen isotope
left hydrogen at very nearly one, so printed tables kept their values
reflected the number of protons that make an atom an oxygen atom
made oxygen combine with a wider range of elements than hydrogen did
was the value the Swedish chemist had proposed for oxygen in the first place
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 gives the reason outright: sixteen was adopted for the unsentimental reason that it left hydrogen at very nearly one and preserved the look of the tables already in print. The tempting trap is the wide-combining property of oxygen, which the same paragraph does state, but as the reason for choosing oxygen at all, not for choosing the number sixteen.

distractors.why: This borrows the single-isotope scale from paragraph 7, which was defined thirty years later; it cannot explain a nineteenth-century choice.
Paragraph 6 does say protons fix an element's identity, but the passage never ties oxygen's assigned value to a proton count.
A true statement from the same paragraph, but it answers a different question: it explains why oxygen rather than hydrogen, not why sixteen rather than one hundred.
Paragraph 4 says he proposed one hundred, so this reverses what the passage states.

questions.stem: The passage reports that the physical and chemical scales differed by approximately:
options: 16 parts per million
40 parts per million
275 parts per million
1,000 parts per million
30,000 parts per million
questions.explanation: Paragraph 7 states the gap as roughly 275 parts per million, about three hundredths of a percent. The 40 figure is the decoy: paragraph 10 uses it for a different quantity, the shift caused by moving to the carbon scale.

distractors.why: Sixteen is the value assigned to oxygen on both scales; it is not a measure of the gap between them.
Paragraph 10 gives 40 parts per million as the size of the later change to carbon, not the gap between the two oxygen scales.
This is nearly four times the gap the passage states.
This is three percent, and it misplaces the decimal by two orders of magnitude: the passage says three hundredths of a percent.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the practical difficulty with hydrogen as the reference was that:
options: hydrogen atoms vary in mass from one sample to another
chemists of the period could not weigh a single atom of any element
hydrogen's assigned value of one had to be revised once the isotopes were discovered
hydrogen combines with few elements, and its compounds were awkward to weigh
hydrogen is not in fact the lightest element
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 names both halves of the difficulty: a modest range of partner elements, and compounds that were often gases hard to trap and weigh, so a determination took several error-adding steps. The inability to weigh a single atom is the attractive wrong answer because paragraph 2 does state it, but it was true of every element and so explains nothing about hydrogen in particular.

distractors.why: Variation between samples is the oxygen problem of paragraphs 6 and 8; the passage never attributes it to hydrogen.
True, and stated in paragraph 2, but it applied equally to every element and is not the reason hydrogen was abandoned.
The passage never says hydrogen's value was revised for isotopes; the revision it describes came from changing the reference substance.
Paragraph 3 says plainly that hydrogen is the lightest element, so this contradicts the text.

questions.stem: The passage indicates that the carbon standard was acceptable to chemists mainly because:
options: the change it forced on published atomic weights was too small to matter
carbon was already the working reference inside mass spectrometry
carbon's common isotope is a single isotope and therefore exactly reproducible
carbon is more abundant than oxygen in ordinary laboratory samples
the two international unions had already voted to adopt it
questions.explanation: Paragraph 10 marks this reason as the decisive one for chemists: a shift of about forty parts per million left the printed tables standing. The other two virtues listed in that paragraph are real, but the passage assigns them to the physicists' principle and to laboratory practice, not to the chemists' objection.

distractors.why: Stated in paragraph 10, but as a convenience of instrument practice, not as the reason chemists could accept the change.
Also stated in paragraph 10, and expressly credited there to the physicists' principle rather than to the chemists' concern.
The passage never compares the abundance of carbon and oxygen in laboratory samples.
Paragraph 11 places the votes in 1960 and 1961, after the proposal had won its argument, so this reverses the order of events.

questions.stem: The passage credits the carbon standard with all of the following features EXCEPT:
options: It rests on a single isotope and can therefore be reproduced exactly.
It was already serving as a reference inside mass spectrometry.
It required only a very small revision of published atomic weights.
It assigns the reference isotope the value twelve exactly.
It replaced hydrogen as the reference substance of the scale.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 10 supplies the first four features directly. The fifth reverses the story: the substance carbon replaced was oxygen, which had itself displaced hydrogen a century earlier, as paragraphs 3 and 4 describe.

distractors.why: Paragraph 10 gives this as the feature that honours the physicists' principle.
Paragraph 10 states that carbon-bearing fragments were already convenient markers in mass spectrometry.
Paragraph 10 puts the revision at about forty parts per million, below the precision of most tables.
Paragraph 10 assigns the common carbon isotope the value twelve exactly; this is the easiest of the four to tick off.

questions.stem: The passage presents all of the following as reasons the oxygen reference had to be abandoned EXCEPT:
options: The composition of natural oxygen varies slightly with its source.
Two scales were in use under a single name.
Published conversion factors invited mistakes.
Oxygen compounds had become too difficult to purify and weigh.
Oxygen is not one kind of atom but three.
questions.explanation: Paragraphs 6 to 9 supply the other four difficulties. The keyed option contradicts paragraph 4, which praises oxygen compounds as stable solids that are easily purified and easily weighed; that convenience was never in dispute.

distractors.why: Paragraph 8 gives this as the serious objection, and says it was what forced a decision.
Paragraph 7 describes exactly this: two scales existing under one name.
Paragraph 9 says a conversion factor guarantees that somebody will eventually forget to apply it.
Paragraph 6 states it outright, which makes this the easiest option to verify and discard.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: The discovery of isotopes made exact atomic weights impossible to assign.
A measurement standard is a convention, judged by whether it can be reproduced.
Physicists and chemists use incompatible methods and therefore reach incompatible results.
Carbon is the best conceivable reference for the atomic weight scale.
The discovery of isotopes was the central event of twentieth-century chemistry.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 announces the theme and paragraph 12 restates it: the point of a standard is to be rebuildable by strangers from written instructions, not to be natural or beautiful, and paragraph 8 makes reproducibility rather than size of error the decisive test. The strongest decoy claims carbon is the best possible reference, which the passage never argues; paragraph 11 says explicitly that the winning proposal was not the most principled one.

distractors.why: The passage describes the scale being repaired, not abandoned, and carbon at twelve is still exact.
The two disciplines did split, but paragraph 11 shows them agreeing; the split is an episode in the argument, not its conclusion.
Paragraph 11 denies this directly: the carbon proposal won because it was cheap for both sides, not because it was best in principle.
The passage treats the discovery as the event that exposed a hidden assumption, and makes no claim about its rank among chemical discoveries.

questions.stem: Which sequence puts the references and scales in the order the passage gives them?
options: Hydrogen at one; oxygen at one hundred; oxygen at sixteen; two scales under one name; carbon at twelve
Oxygen at one hundred; hydrogen at one; oxygen at sixteen; two scales under one name; carbon at twelve
Hydrogen at one; oxygen at sixteen; oxygen at one hundred; two scales under one name; carbon at twelve exactly
Hydrogen at one; oxygen at one hundred; oxygen at sixteen; carbon at twelve; two scales under one name
Two scales under one name; hydrogen at one; oxygen at one hundred; oxygen at sixteen; carbon at twelve
questions.explanation: The passage lays the references out in order: hydrogen at one in paragraph 3, a Swedish chemist's oxygen at one hundred and then the community's oxygen at sixteen in paragraph 4, the split into two scales under one name in paragraph 7, and carbon at twelve in paragraph 10. The two oxygen values are the pair hardest to keep straight, because both sit in one paragraph and the passage marks the change only with the sentence that one hundred did not survive.

distractors.why: Paragraph 3 calls hydrogen at one the first convention, so the Swedish chemist's oxygen at one hundred cannot come before it.
The two oxygen values are reversed: paragraph 4 gives one hundred first, says that figure did not survive, and only then puts the community on sixteen.
Carbon arrives to end the split, not before it; paragraph 10 introduces it as the proposal that broke the deadlock the two scales had created.
There was no scale to divide until one existed: paragraph 7 places the split after oxygen at sixteen had been in use for decades.

questions.stem: Which title best captures the content and emphasis of the passage?
options: Isotopes: Why Atoms of One Element Are Not Alike
A Standard Anyone Can Rebuild: Fixing the Atomic Weight Scale
Oxygen Against Carbon: How Two Disciplines Fell Out Over a Number
The Limits of Precision in Modern Measurement
Nineteenth-Century Chemistry and Its Mistakes
questions.explanation: A good title has to carry both halves of the passage, the narrative of how the reference was chosen and the argument of paragraphs 1 and 12 that a standard exists to be rebuilt by anyone. The quarrel title is the half-right trap: it names paragraphs 7 to 9 accurately and leaves out the thesis the passage opens and closes with.

distractors.why: Isotopes occupy one paragraph and serve the argument; a title built on them misses the subject.
Accurate for the middle of the passage only, and the passage ends in agreement rather than quarrel.
The passage is about reproducibility and convention, not about how precise measurement can become.
The passage defends the nineteenth-century choice as practical, so this title misstates its attitude.

questions.stem: The discussion of the unstated assumption in paragraph 5 serves primarily to:
options: argue that the chemists of the period were careless
introduce the definition of an isotope
identify the assumption the oxygen standard rested on, and why it stayed hidden
establish that oxygen combines with nearly every element
show that hydrogen would have made a better reference than oxygen after all
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 names the premise the standard rested on, that an element is a single kind of atom, and says it stayed invisible because nobody saw it was a premise. That prepares the reversal in paragraph 6 and explains why the reversal was a surprise. The carelessness reading is the trap: the paragraph states that nobody saw the assumption was a premise, which excuses the chemists rather than blaming them.

distractors.why: The paragraph says nobody saw the assumption was a premise, which is an explanation rather than an accusation.
The definition arrives in paragraph 6; paragraph 5 prepares the ground for it without naming isotopes.
That point belongs to paragraph 4 and is not what paragraph 5 is doing.
The passage never revives hydrogen; paragraph 3 explains why it was abandoned.

questions.stem: Paragraph 9 contributes to the passage mainly by:
options: showing that the conversion factors between the scales were arithmetically incorrect
describing how a mass spectrometer separates isotopes
explaining why the composition of natural oxygen varies with its source
setting out the remedies tried before carbon, and why each one fell short
identifying which of the two disciplines was ultimately proved right
questions.explanation: Paragraph 9 names two responses, conversion factors and mutual persuasion, and dismisses both as evasions, which is what makes the carbon proposal in paragraph 10 look necessary rather than arbitrary. The arithmetic reading inverts the text: the paragraph concedes that the conversion works and objects that it is a confession, not that it is wrong.

distractors.why: The paragraph grants that arithmetic always works; its objection is to what the factor admits, not to its accuracy.
No such description appears anywhere in the passage.
That explanation belongs to paragraph 8.
The paragraph calls both disciplines correct, so it settles nothing between them.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the practice of publishing conversion factors between the two scales is best described as:
options: admiring of their ingenuity
indifferent to their consequences
hostile to the point of open contempt
undecided about their merits
critical, but granting that they work
questions.explanation: Paragraph 9 calls the practice an evasion and a confession rather than a solution, yet allows in the same breath that arithmetic always works. That combination of a clear objection with an explicit concession is criticism, not contempt and not indifference. Readers who register only the word evasion reach for the harshest option.

distractors.why: The paragraph offers no praise for the method at all.
The author's complaint is precisely about a consequence, that somebody will forget to apply the factor.
Too strong for a paragraph that concedes the method works and treats it as a reasonable first try.
The author is not undecided; the verdict of evasion is delivered in the paragraph's first sentence.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the nineteenth-century chemists who built the scale on oxygen is best described as:
options: respectful of their practical reasoning
impatient with their lack of rigour
indifferent to their contribution
gently mocking of their conclusions
admiring of their foresight about isotopes
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 calls their choice unsentimental and draws a favourable lesson from it, and paragraph 5 says the assumption they relied on was invisible because nobody saw it was a premise. The passage credits their practicality while noting what they could not have known. The foresight option is half right: the approval is genuine, but the passage says the isotopes took them completely by surprise.

distractors.why: The passage excuses rather than scolds them, saying the assumption could not be seen while it held.
Two full paragraphs are given to explaining and justifying their reasoning.
Nothing in the passage ridicules them; the word applied to their reasoning is unsentimental, which is praise here.
Paragraph 6 shows the isotopes arriving as a surprise, so foresight is exactly what they lacked.

questions.stem: If the isotopic composition of natural oxygen had been identical everywhere, it follows from the passage that:
options: physicists and chemists would never have found themselves working on two separate scales
oxygen would have turned out to have only one isotope
no revision of published atomic weights would ever have been needed
the two scales would still differ, but the chemists' reference would be reproducible
the carbon standard would have been unnecessary for the physicists as well
questions.explanation: Paragraph 7 traces the gap between the scales to the difference between a single isotope and a mixture, and paragraph 8 traces the reproducibility complaint to variation between sources. Remove the variation and the second complaint goes, while the first, which does not depend on it, remains. The tempting answer erases the split entirely, but a uniform mixture is still a mixture and still weighs more than its lightest component.

distractors.why: The split came from the mixture weighing more than the single isotope, which a uniform composition would not change.
Uniform proportions of three isotopes are still three isotopes, so this does not follow.
The move to carbon still altered every published weight, by about forty parts per million.
The physicists' objection was to using a mixture at all, and paragraph 9 presents it as independent of where the sample came from.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly implies that the numerical value given to a reference substance:
options: is determined by the element's number of protons
is chosen partly to avoid disturbing values already in use
must always be a whole number
cannot be revised once tables have been published
is fixed by whichever instrument is most precise at the time
questions.explanation: Two separate episodes point the same way: sixteen was chosen in paragraph 4 because it kept hydrogen near one and the printed tables intact, and carbon was accepted in paragraph 10 because the resulting change was too small to disturb the tables. Continuity with existing numbers is a criterion in both. The absolute options are the classic trap; the passage shows values being revised, so no rule forbidding revision can be inferred.

distractors.why: Paragraph 6 ties protons to an element's identity, never to the number assigned to a reference.
One hundred, sixteen and twelve are all whole numbers, but the passage gives no reason why a reference value must be one.
Paragraph 10 describes exactly such a revision being made and accepted.
Instruments exposed the problem; the passage shows the value being settled by agreement, not by an instrument.

questions.stem: Which finding, if established, would most weaken the objection raised in paragraph 8?
options: Most chemists at the bench never noticed any difference between the two scales.
The gap between the two scales was smaller than two hundred and seventy-five parts per million.
Oxygen from air, seawater and minerals proves to have identical isotopic composition.
Carbon's isotopic composition also varies between natural sources.
Mass spectrometers became cheap enough for ordinary chemistry laboratories to buy.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 8 objects that the chemists' reference drifted with its source and so could not be reproduced exactly. A demonstration that every source gives the same composition removes the drift and with it the objection. The two size-based options are decoys: the paragraph concedes that the gap was negligible for bench work and insists that the size of the gap is not the point.

distractors.why: Paragraph 8 concedes this in its first sentence and argues that it is beside the point.
The objection is about reproducibility, not magnitude, so shrinking the gap leaves it untouched.
This would bear on the later choice of carbon, not on whether the oxygen reference drifted.
Cheaper instruments would let chemists see the drift more easily, which does nothing to remove it.

questions.stem: A committee must choose a reference substance for a new measurement scale. Based on the passage, the author would most likely favour:
options: a naturally occurring mixture that any laboratory can obtain in bulk
whichever candidate the largest research community already prefers
a single artefact kept in a secure vault and consulted whenever disputes arise
a candidate chosen so that not one published value anywhere has to change
a pure substance anyone can reproduce, even if adoption forces small revisions
questions.explanation: The two criteria the passage endorses are reproducibility, argued in paragraphs 8 and 12, and a cost small enough for the people who must use the standard to bear, argued in paragraphs 10 and 11. Only one option carries both. Demanding that nothing change at all is the near miss: the passage accepts a revision of every published weight precisely because it was small.

distractors.why: This is the oxygen mistake of paragraphs 6 and 8, where a natural mixture drifted with its source.
Paragraph 11 states that the winning proposal was not the one urged by the more powerful discipline.
Paragraph 12 treats the vault artefact as the model modern standards have moved away from.
Paragraph 10 shows a change of about forty parts per million being accepted; a demand for zero change is stricter than the passage.
